john-kiriakou.body_append:
## The Rhodian family and the 26 percent Cretan

On *The Untold Stories* in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said all four of his grandparents were from Rhodes — his father's parents from Yalisos in the north of the island, his mother's from Katavia, the southernmost village. His mother was one of nine, and Kiriakou has twenty-seven first cousins on that side.<Cite t="02:38" /><Cite t="03:08" /><Cite t="06:16" /> A 23andMe test he took after being invited to speak at a *Cretans of the Diaspora* conference came back 26 percent Cretan — a heritage a cousin then told him he had known about all along, from an ancestral village Kiriakou had misheard as Kithnos but was in fact Kiti.<Cite t="03:40" /><Cite t="04:11" />

## Yaya's Arhangelos veto

Kiriakou tells a tight family story from his early twenties: he had wanted to ask out a good-looking young woman from the Rhodian village of Arhangelos, whom he had met at his cousin's bridal-gown boutique in Warren, Ohio. His grandmother, on being told the plan, put her foot down: *"I don't interfere, but I'm putting my foot down on this — she's from Arhangelos … people from Arhangelos have big heads and they lie, and they care only about property."* Kiriakou did not ask her out.<Cite t="04:43" /><Cite t="05:13" /><Cite t="05:45" />

## Modern Greek at the DC consortium

As an undergraduate at George Washington University, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) tried to enrol in Modern Greek at Georgetown through the DC university consortium and was told he was already too far behind. Kiriakou protested that he had spoken Greek at home. The professor — the dean of the school of languages and linguistics — asked him to speak, then delivered his verdict: *"Your Greek is terrible … you speak in this weird 1930s-era Dodecanese slang. When did your people come over?"* When Kiriakou said 1931 and 1934, the professor answered *"and you're probably from — what, Rhodes?"* — and put him in the beginner class.<Cite t="06:46" /><Cite t="07:17" /><Cite t="07:47" />

kiriakou-recruitment-attempts.body_append:
## The undercover graduate-school adviser

On *The Untold Stories* in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said the man who eventually recruited him into the [CIA](/wiki/cia) had spent Kiriakou's George Washington University graduate years working undercover as his academic adviser. *"My adviser in graduate school turned out to be a CIA officer undercover as an adviser. And he spotted me and thought that I would be good."* Kiriakou was, on his own count, the only student the adviser recruited at GW; the arrangement — with a case officer stationed on-campus specifically to identify candidates — predated the 1993 Equal Employment Opportunity Act reforms that moved the CIA's front door to a public website, at which point applications rose from 250 per opening pre-9/11 to about 2,500 per opening post-9/11.<Cite t="12:26" /><Cite t="12:58" /><Cite t="13:28" />

saddam-hussein.body_append:
## The mob-boss framework

[John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said on *The Untold Stories* in July 2026 that his own analytic framework, worked out over seven-and-a-half years as [Saddam Hussein](/wiki/saddam-hussein)'s classified CIA biographer in the office of leadership analysis, was that Saddam was best understood not as *"crazy"* but as a mob boss. *"Crazy is just different"* — a category label he says people use as a substitute for policy disagreement. Saddam, on Kiriakou's rendering, was *"extraordinarily quick to use violence"* and applied a mob-boss's terror repertoire: cut out a critic's tongue and nail it to the front door of his house so *"nobody in the neighbourhood was going to speak out"*; move a popular general to a distant ambassadorship rather than allow the political threat to consolidate.<Cite t="14:32" /><Cite t="15:04" /><Cite t="15:34" />

## The stage-purge video

Kiriakou reaches for the freely available footage of the day Saddam took power as the single best summary of the leadership technique. Sitting on stage in a small theatre, cigar in hand, Saddam announced that *"a plot against the revolution"* had been uncovered among the assembled generals. One by one he read names; each general stood, protested his innocence, and was walked out by Saddam's brother Barzan Al-Tikriti to the sound of a gunshot. The pattern broke only when one named general jumped up and confessed to the (non-existent) plot outright. Roughly a dozen generals were killed that day. There had been no plot; the pattern of terror it produced, Kiriakou says, was the point: *"it so cowed them that nobody dared to challenge Saddam."*<Cite t="16:04" /><Cite t="16:36" /><Cite t="17:06" />

cofer-black.body_append:
## The morning of 11 September 2001

On *The Untold Stories* in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said he had been scheduled that Tuesday morning for a 9 a.m. meeting at the White House with [Condoleezza Rice](/wiki/condoleezza-rice), then National Security Adviser, in the company of [Cofer Black](/wiki/cofer-black), the director of the CIA's counter-terrorism centre. Kiriakou walked across the hall to Black's office to tell him the car was ready. Black's secretary — this being *"the days before you could watch TV on a computer"* — had a small television on her desk; when Kiriakou reached the desk one of the towers of the World Trade Center was already burning. *"I said, 'what happened to the World Trade Center?' And she said, 'a plane flew into it.'"*<Cite t="24:58" /><Cite t="25:30" />

revolutionary-organization-17-november.body_append:
## More dangerous than Pakistan

On *The Untold Stories* in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said his 1998–2000 tour in Athens working the [17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november) target was the most dangerous period of his career — more dangerous, he said, than his post-9/11 tour running counter-terrorism operations in Pakistan. The reason, he said, was that between the mid-1970s and 2002 the United States spent more money on security in Athens than it did in Beirut, and 17 November had operated for a quarter-century without a single member being caught or even identified: *"is it the guy you're sitting next to, is it the guy in traffic, is it the guy on the motorcycle weaving through traffic and coming up alongside you — you just didn't know."* When he originally applied for the post, Kiriakou said, it was meant to be a broad Athens counter-terrorism assignment covering the [Abu Nidal Organisation](/wiki/abu-nidal), the Libyans, the PFLP, the PFLP-GC, the DFLP and Islamic Jihad; in practice 90 percent of the work was 17 November because — post-Oslo Accords — the Arab groups had gone quiet.<Cite t="21:50" /><Cite t="22:21" /><Cite t="23:23" /><Cite t="23:54" />
